articles.title: 'Can't control the weather': Sadness as Macy's Thanksgiving parade postponed
articles.summary: Macy's postpones its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York because of severe weather.
articles.body:
Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York because of severe weather. It is the first time the parade has been postponed due to weather.

Fans and volunteers voiced their disappointment over the postponement, with one remarking: 'We can't control the weather!'

Preparations to hold the iconic holiday celebration, known for its massive balloons that float among the city's skyscrapers, had already begun when the forecast for heavy rain and strong winds on Thursday led to the delay.

It is hoped the parade will take place on Saturday instead.

articles.title: Nvidia reveals Blackwell B200 GPU, the ‘world’s most powerful chip’ for AI
articles.summary: Perhaps Nvidia is about to extend its lead in the AI chip race — with the new Blackwell B200 GPU and GB200 “superchip.”
articles.body: Nvidia’s must-have H100 AI chip made it a multitrillion-dollar company, one that may be worth more than Alphabet and Amazon, and competitors have been fighting to catch up. But perhaps Nvidia is about to extend its lead — with the new Blackwell B200 GPU and GB200 “superchip.” [Image: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang holds up his new GPU on the left, next to an H100 on the right, from the GTC livestream. Nvidia says the new B200 GPU offers up to 20 petaflops of FP4 horsepower from its 208 billion transistors. Also, it says, a GB200 that combines two of those GPUs with a single Grace CPU can offer 30 times the performance for LLM inference workloads while also potentially being substantially more efficient. It “reduces cost and energy consumption by up to 25x” over an H100, says Nvidia, though there’s a questionmark around cost — Nvidia’s CEO has suggested each GPU might cost between $30,000 and $40,000. Training a 1.8 trillion parameter model would have previously taken 8,000 Hopper GPUs and 15 megawatts of power, Nvidia claims. Today, Nvidia’s CEO says 2,000 Blackwell GPUs can do it while consuming just four megawatts. On a GPT-3 LLM benchmark with 175 billion parameters, Nvidia says the GB200 has a somewhat more modest seven times the performance of an H100, and Nvidia says it offers four times the training speed. [Image: Here’s what one GB200 looks like. Two GPUs, one CPU, one board. Nvidia told journalists one of the key improvements is a second-gen transformer engine that doubles the compute, bandwidth, and model size by using four bits for each neuron instead of eight (thus, the 20 petaflops of FP4 I mentioned earlier). A second key difference only comes when you link up huge numbers of these GPUs: a next-gen NVLink switch that lets 576 GPUs talk to each other, with 1.8 terabytes per second of bidirectional bandwidth. That required Nvidia to build an entire new network switch chip, one with 50 billion transistors and some of its own onboard compute: 3.6 teraflops of FP8, says Nvidia. [Image: Nvidia says it’s adding both FP4 and FP6 with Blackwell. Previously, Nvidia says, a cluster of just 16 GPUs would spend 60 percent of their time communicating with one another and only 40 percent actually computing. Nvidia is counting on companies to buy large quantities of these GPUs, of course, and is packaging them in larger designs, like the GB200 NVL72, which plugs 36 CPUs and 72 GPUs into a single liquid-cooled rack for a total of 720 petaflops of AI training performance or 1,440 petaflops (aka 1.4 exaflops) of inference. It has nearly two miles of cables inside, with 5,000 individual cables. [Image: The GB200 NVL72. Each tray in the rack contains either two GB200 chips or two NVLink switches, with 18 of the former and nine of the latter per rack. In total, Nvidia says one of these racks can support a 27-trillion parameter model. GPT-4 is rumored to be around a 1.7-trillion parameter model. The company says Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Oracle are all already planning to offer the NVL72 racks in their cloud service offerings, though it’s not clear how many they’re buying. And of course, Nvidia is happy to offer companies the rest of the solution, too. Here’s the DGX Superpod for DGX GB200, which combines eight systems in one for a total of 288 CPUs, 576 GPUs, 240TB of memory, and 11.5 exaflops of FP4 computing. [Image: Nvidia says its systems can scale to tens of thousands of the GB200 superchips, connected together with 800Gbps networking with its new Quantum-X800 InfiniBand (for up to 144 connections) or Spectrum-X800 ethernet (for up to 64 connections). We don’t expect to hear anything about new gaming GPUs today, as this news is coming out of Nvidia’s GPU Technology Conference, which is usually almost entirely focused on GPU computing and AI, not gaming. But the Blackwell GPU architecture will likely also power a future RTX 50-series lineup of desktop graphics cards. Update, March 19th: Added Nvidia CEO estimate that the new GPUs might cost up to $40K each.

articles.title: Nvidia announces Blackwell Ultra GB300 and Vera Rubin, its next AI ‘superchips’
articles.summary: Nvidia has announced the Blackwell Ultra GB300, its latest AI chip for AI server businesses.
articles.body: Nvidia now makes $2,300 in profit every second on the back of the AI revolution. Its data center business is so gigantic, even its networking hardware now rakes in more money than its gaming GPUs. Now, the company is announcing the AI GPUs that it hopes will extend its commanding lead: the Blackwell Ultra GB300, which will ship in the second half of this year, the Vera Rubin for the second half of next year, and the Rubin Ultra that will arrive in the second half of 2027. This year’s Blackwell Ultra isn’t what we originally expected when Nvidia said last year that it would begin producing new AI chips on a yearly cadence, faster than ever before, as Blackwell Ultra is not on a new architecture. But Nvidia quickly moved on from Blackwell Ultra during today’s GTC keynote to reveal that next architecture, Vera Rubin, whose full rack should offer 3.3x the performance of a comparable Blackwell Ultra one. [Image: Nvidia’s new AI chip roadmap as of March 2025. Nvidia isn’t making it easy to tell how much better Blackwell Ultra is than the original Blackwell. In a prebriefing with journalists, Nvidia revealed a single Ultra chip will offer the same 20 petaflops of AI performance as Blackwell, but now with 288GB of HBM3e memory rather than 192GB of the same. Meanwhile, a Blackwell Ultra DGX GB300 “Superpod” cluster will offer the same 288 CPUs, 576 GPUs and 11.5 exaflops of FP4 computing as the Blackwell version, but with 300TB of memory rather than 240TB. [Image: Mostly, Nvidia compared its new Blackwell Ultra to the H100, the 2022 chip that originally built Nvidia’s AI fortunes and from which leading companies might presumably want to upgrade: there, Nvidia says it offers 1.5x the FP4 inference and can dramatically speed up “AI reasoning,” with the NVL72 cluster capable of running an interactive copy of DeepSeek-R1 671B that can provide answers in just 10 seconds instead of the H100’s 1.5 minutes. Nvidia says that’s because it can process 1,000 tokens per second, 10 times that of Nvidia’s 2022 chips. But one intriguing difference is that some companies will be able to buy a single Blackwell Ultra chip: Nvidia announced a desktop computer called the DGX Station with a single GB300 Blackwell Ultra on board, 784GB of unified system memory, built-in 800Gbps Nvidia networking, and the promised 20 petaflops of AI performance. Asus, Dell, and HP will join Boxx, Lambda, and Supermicro in selling versions of the desktop. [Image: A DGX Station desktop motherboard with Nvidia’s Blackwell Ultra on board. Nvidia will also offer a single rack called the GB300 NVL72 that offers 1.1 exaflops of FP4, 20TB of HBM memory, 40TB of “fast memory,” and 130TB/sec of NVLink bandwidth and 14.4 TB/sec networking. But Vera Rubin and Rubin Ultra may dramatically improve on that performance when they arrive in 2026 and 2027. Rubin has 50 petaflops of FP4, up from 20 petaflops in Blackwell. Rubin Ultra will feature a chip that effectively contains two Rubin GPUs connected together, with twice the performance at 100 petaflops of FP4 and nearly quadruple the memory at 1TB. A full NVL576 rack of Rubin Ultra claims to offer 15 exaflops of FP4 inference and 5 exaflops of FP8 training for what Nvidia says is 14x the performance of the Blackwell Ultra rack it’s shipping this year. Find other specs by blowing up the images below: [Image: [Image: Nvidia says it has already shipped $11 billion worth of Blackwell revenue; the top four buyers alone have purchased 1.8 million Blackwell chips so far in 2025. Nvidia’s pushing these new chips — and all its AI chips — as essential to the future of computing and is trying to argue today that companies will need more and more computing power, not less as some assumed after DeepSeek shook up investor assumptions and sent Nvidia’s stock price tumbling. At the Nvidia GPU technology conference today, founder and CEO Jensen Huang says the industry needs “100 times more than then we thought we needed this time last year” to keep up with demand. Huang says Nvidia’s next architecture after Vera Rubin, coming 2028, will be named Feynman — presumably after Richard Feynman, the famous theoretical physicist. He said some of pioneering astronomer Vera Rubin’s family was in the audience today.

articles.title: Anthropic will face a class-action lawsuit from US authors
articles.summary: A California federal judge ruled Thursday that three authors suing Anthropic over copyright infringement can bring a class action lawsuit representing all U.S. writers whose work was allegedly downloaded from libraries of pirated works.
articles.body: A California federal judge ruled Thursday that three authors suing Anthropic over copyright infringement can bring a class action lawsuit representing all US writers whose work was allegedly downloaded from libraries of pirated works. The filing alleges that Anthropic, the Amazon-backed OpenAI competitor behind the chatbot Claude, “violated the Copyright Act by doing Napster-style downloading of millions of works.” It alleges that the company downloaded as many as seven million copies of books from libraries of pirated works. The new ruling impacts a lawsuit filed last August by authors Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber, and Kirk Wallace Johnson, who alleged that Anthropic had “built a multibillion-dollar business by stealing hundreds of thousands of copyrighted books.” Late last month, a federal judge sided with Anthropic to rule that training its AI models on legally-purchased books was fair use but noted the company would need to face a separate trial for using allegedly pirated books. It also follows the lawsuit Reddit filed against Anthropic last month, claiming that the AI company’s bots had accessed Reddit more than 100,000 times since last July, after Anthropic had said it blocked them from doing so. The authors’ lawsuit is part of a growing trend of media outlets, platforms, companies, and creatives either suing AI companies over copyright infringement — for instance, Universal Music’s 2023 lawsuit against Anthropic over “systematic and widespread infringement of their copyrighted song lyrics” — or partnering up with them to willingly provide AI training data in order to get a slice of the profits.

articles.title: Anthropic to pay $1.5 billion to authors in landmark AI settlement
articles.summary: A settlement between Anthropic and authors over books used to train its AI would pay out “at least” $1.5 billion to resolve a class-action copyright lawsuit.
articles.body: In what’s potentially the first major payout to creatives whose work was used to train AI systems, Anthropic has reached an agreement to pay “at least” a staggering $1.5 billion, plus interest, to authors to settle its class-action lawsuit. The amount breaks down to smaller payouts expected to be approximately $3,000 per book or work. Lawyers for the plaintiffs said it’s “believed to be the largest publicly reported recovery in the history of US copyright litigation.” “This result is nothing short of remarkable,” the legal filing states. The settlement is subject to court approval, and a hearing will take place on September 8th. According to a press release, the final amount could be higher, in that approximately 500,000 works will likely be paid out, but if the total is higher than that, Anthropic will pay an additional $3,000 per work, and it all depends on the number of claims submitted. As part of the settlement, Anthropic must also destroy the original files it downloaded and any copies. “The settlement only releases claims based on past acts – it does not give Anthropic a license or permission for future AI training and it does not release any claims that arise after August 25, 2025,” the release stated. The landmark decision is part of a year-long saga. In August 2024, three authors — Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber, and Kirk Wallace Johnson — alleged that Anthropic had “built a multibillion-dollar business by stealing hundreds of thousands of copyrighted books.” Over the summer, a federal judge handed Anthropic a small win, ruling that the company was within its legal rights to train its AI models on legally purchased books. But the judge also said that Anthropic would need to face a separate trial for its alleged use of pirated books. In July, a California federal judge ruled that the authors could bring a class action lawsuit representing all US writers whose work allegedly came from libraries of pirated books downloaded by Anthropic. And late last month, Anthropic said it had settled the class action lawsuit — but we didn’t know the terms until now. “In June, the District Court issued a landmark ruling on AI development and copyright law, finding that Anthropic’s approach to training AI models constitutes fair use,” Aparna Sridhar, Anthropic’s deputy general counsel, told The Verge in a statement. “Today’s settlement, if approved, will resolve the plaintiffs’ remaining legacy claims. We remain committed to developing safe AI systems that help people and organizations extend their capabilities, advance scientific discovery, and solve complex problems.” The settlement is especially noteworthy during a time of mounting lawsuits against AI companies over copyright infringement from media outlets, platforms, creatives, and companies — and, at the same time, an increasing number of partnerships with those same AI companies from companies and media outlets willing to provide data to train AI systems in order to get a piece of the pie. It’s not the only legal action Anthropic has faced in recent years. This summer, Reddit filed suit against Anthropic, claiming that the AI company’s bots had accessed Reddit more than 100,000 times since July 2024, after Anthropic had said it blocked them from doing so. And in 2023, Universal Music sued Anthropic over “systematic and widespread infringement of their copyrighted song lyrics.” For this case, authors and rightsholders may visit AnthropicCopyrightSettlement.com, the release stated, a website that “which gives potential class members an option to provide contact information to Class Counsel.” “In the coming weeks, and if the court preliminarily approves the settlement, the website will provide to find a full and easily searchable listing of all works covered by the settlement and information for class members about their options and rights regarding the settlement,” the release said. articles.title: Canonical lays out a plan for AI in Ubuntu Linux
articles.summary: Ubuntu developer Canonical has announced plans to start adding AI features to the popular Linux distribution over the next year.
articles.body: One of the most popular Linux distributions is about to get an influx of AI features. As reported by Phoronix, Jon Seager, VP of engineering at Ubuntu developer Canonical, shared a blog post on Monday detailing plans to add AI features to the Linux distro over the next year. As the post states, the AI features “will come in two forms: first as a means of enhancing existing OS functionality with AI models in the background, and latterly in the form of ‘AI native’ features and workflows for those who want them.” These features will range from accessibility tools like improved speech-to-text and text-to-speech to agentic AI features for tasks like troubleshooting or personal automation. According to Seager, Canonical will be prioritizing model transparency and local inference when adding these AI features. Behind the scenes, Canonical is also encouraging its engineers to use AI more, but Seager noted that “I will not be measuring people at Canonical by how much they use AI, but rather continue to measure them on how well they deliver.” Seager goes on to add that AI features could potentially help new users navigate the “famously fragmented” Linux desktop ecosystem: “If we’re careful about how we employ LLMs in a system context, they could demystify the capabilities of a modern Linux workstation and bring them to a much wider audience.”

articles.title: Anthropic’s $1.5 billion book piracy settlement approved by judge
articles.summary: A federal judge has approved Anthropic’s $1.5 billion settlement with authors who accused it of stealing their copyrighted books.
articles.body: A federal judge has signed off on Anthropic’s $1.5 billion class action settlement with authors who accused the company of training its AI models on copyrighted books, as reported earlier by Reuters. In an order on Monday, Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín writes that the settlement will provide “meaningful relief,” offering authors around $3,000 for each book allegedly pirated by Anthropic. The $1.5 billion settlement is the “largest known copyright recovery in history,” according to the law firm representing the plaintiffs. A group of authors — Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber, and Kirk Wallace Johnson — first filed a copyright lawsuit against Anthropic in 2024. While the now-retired Judge William Alsup granted Anthropic a partial victory last year, he approved a separate class action lawsuit claiming the company engaged in the “Napster-style downloading of millions of works.” Anthropic agreed to a $1.5 billion settlement in September 2025, to which Judge Alsup later granted preliminary approval. “We are pleased that more than 91% of authors and publishers covered by the settlement have claimed their share of the payment,” Anthropic general counsel Aparna Sridhar tells Reuters. “We’re looking forward ​to bringing this matter to a close.” Anthropic is still facing copyright lawsuits from Chicken Soup for the Soul and several other authors who argue that $3,000 per book isn’t enough.

articles.title: OpenAI and Anthropic Insiders Fear Their Next AI Models Are Too Dangerous to Release
articles.summary: Employees at both AI labs reportedly question whether their strongest models should ever reach the public, as researchers struggle to keep increasingly capab...
articles.body:
Employees at OpenAI and Anthropic are increasingly concerned that their companies' most advanced AI models may never be safe enough for public release, according to a Tuesday report by Axios citing more than two dozen sources familiar with internal discussions.

Some researchers believe the technical problems can eventually be solved. Others reportedly want the companies to stop training more intelligent models altogether.

The report comes two days after Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang warned that humanity might be approaching a point where it can no longer effectively supervise artificial intelligence. Wang argued that decisions made over the next year could determine whether humans retain control over increasingly autonomous, self-improving AI systems.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

His warning followed Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge's announcement that an unreleased version of Claude had helped him prove the Riemann Hypothesis, a mathematical problem that had frustrated researchers for 167 years.

The same intellectual abilities that make these models so valuable for scientific research are making them harder to supervise. A model capable of spotting something that generations of mathematicians missed could conceivably spot weaknesses in a safety system that its developers overlooked.

When smarter AI becomes harder to control

One of the biggest problems facing AI researchers involves reinforcement learning, a training technique that rewards models for successfully completing tasks. It's largely responsible for the impressive reasoning abilities of modern AI systems, but it can also teach them to cheat.

Researchers call this reward hacking . A model might, for example, manipulate the software responsible for grading its work instead of actually solving the problem it was assigned.

Anthropic encountered a version of this problem in February, when researchers reversed three days of training on Claude Mythos Preview after discovering undesirable behaviors. An internal review later flagged more than 10% of its active training environments for problems that included opportunities for cheating and incorrectly configured tasks.

Another problem involves chain-of-thought monitoring, which allows researchers to inspect the intermediate reasoning an AI generates before producing an answer or taking an action. Some unreleased models are increasingly capable of obscuring that reasoning or generating misleading explanations that satisfy their monitors.

In other words, the explanation researchers receive may no longer accurately reflect how the model arrived at its decision.

OpenAI has already experienced the real-world consequences of inadequate containment. The company acknowledged that an internal research model was primarily responsible for compromising AI development platform Hugging Face while pursuing a difficult task.

Keeping the smartest models away from ChatGPT and Claude users would therefore address only part of the problem.

"Keeping a model internal doesn't make it safe," an Anthropic spokesperson told Axios .

OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed Sunday that AI developers agree on common limits to model development, based partly on perplexity—a mathematical measure of how accurately a model predicts subsequent pieces of text, with lower scores indicating better predictions.

Pachocki argues that companies should agree not to cross certain thresholds until researchers develop more effective ways of monitoring AI behavior. He estimates that AI-assisted research could substantially accelerate the development of new models as early as 2027.

Getting competing companies to voluntarily slow down could prove particularly difficult, especially as investors expect returns on the enormous amounts of money pouring into AI infrastructure. Anthropic itself raised more than $81 billion when it went public last week.

OpenAI said last week that it would suspend training or withhold models again if they failed to satisfy its safety requirements. Anthropic has separately committed to publishing a policy proposal on independent AI evaluators by December 15, followed by a framework addressing the pace of AI development by January 15, 2027.

articles.title: No GPS required: Ukrainian 11th-grader creates AI drone navigation system
articles.summary: GPS jamming is one of modern drone warfare's biggest headaches — a Ukrainian 11th-grader just built an AI guidance system that doesn't need satellites at all
articles.body:

Ukrainian teenager develops drone autopilot capable of operating without GPS signals

11th-grade student Yaroslav Sheiko receives Ukraine's presidential award for drone innovations

Artificial intelligence powers the student's GPS-independent drone navigation technology

A Ukrainian high school student has developed drone technology capable of guiding unmanned aircraft without depending on satellite navigation systems.

Yaroslav Sheiko, an 11th-grade pupil from Poltava, received the presidential distinction known as "The Future of Ukraine" for his engineering achievements.

His work includes an artificial intelligence-powered flight control system and optical-electronic stabilization technology designed for unmanned aerial vehicles.

Sheiko's main innovation involves an autonomous guidance system that allows drones to reach designated destinations without relying on conventional satellite positioning signals.

The technology is designed to help unmanned aircraft maintain their intended flight paths when GPS and other global navigation services become unavailable.

According to information released by Poltava's municipal education department, the student has been developing engineering solutions for unmanned aerial vehicles.

His navigation system enables an aircraft to independently approach a location selected by its operator while flying relatively close to the ground.

This capability addresses a major difficulty facing drone operators when electronic interference disrupts satellite navigation signals during flight.

GPS jamming and spoofing can interfere with conventional navigation equipment, potentially preventing aircraft from maintaining accurate positioning.

Sheiko's work also includes optical-electronic stabilization equipment incorporating artificial intelligence for improved drone control and navigation.

Such equipment can help maintain stable observations and support guidance when conventional satellite-based positioning becomes unreliable.

However, there is no information on the precise sensors, algorithms, or computational hardware powering his navigation system.

Details about its operational testing, navigation accuracy, maximum range, and performance under different environmental conditions have also not been disclosed.

Without further technical details, it remains difficult to determine how his invention compares with existing GPS-independent navigation systems.

Nevertheless, receiving national recognition while still attending secondary school is a major achievement for the young Ukrainian engineer.

Presidential award follows several international science competition victories

The "The Future of Ukraine" distinction adds another achievement to Sheiko's growing record of recognition in engineering and scientific competitions.

He has previously received presidential scholarships on two occasions, recognizing his performance and contributions to scientific research.

The student has also secured first place twice in nationwide competitions organized by Ukraine's Junior Academy of Sciences.

His entries competed within the aerospace and defense technology category, focusing on engineering developments relevant to unmanned systems.

International competitions have also featured his inventions, including the INOVA 2025 International Inventions Show, where he secured a gold medal.

He additionally received a silver medal in the 2025 Hackathon, adding another international achievement to his academic record.

His latest presidential award recognizes his contributions to drone engineering, particularly developments involving autonomous navigation and electronic stabilization.

Ukraine's continuing efforts to maintain drone operations despite electronic interference have also encouraged interest in alternative communication technologies.

The country has been exploring alternatives to Starlink for maintaining drone communications when satellite connectivity becomes unavailable during military operations.

It recently reportedly combined airborne relay systems with Israeli-Italian satellite communications technology to provide alternative links for unmanned aircraft.

While these systems maintain communication with operators, Sheiko's invention addresses another challenge by allowing drones to navigate without GPS signals.

articles.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
articles.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushes back against rivals’ accusations that he favors surrendering human agency to AI, even as leading AI companies increasingly...
articles.body:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should "surrender human free will" to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion "absurd."

"We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security," he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different."

The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have "agency over the future."

Meta's chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we "should not be okay with a 'handover' of society to AI."

"It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement," Wang wrote. "Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully."

But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.

Amodei noted that there's a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that "as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way." As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.

Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, "we may want limits on this process."

Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic's codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic's models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.

In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as "closing the loop."

"As we said publicly in early November, we don't expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding," Amodei wrote.

The problem with "meaningful human supervision or understanding" is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they're being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control.

Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.

In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a "vibes-based commercial and political positioning," disingenuously throwing around phrases like "human control and agency" or "AI should just be a tool" without approaching the AI race any differently.

"Certainly the products that they offer don't differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation," Amodei wrote. "Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards."

articles.title: JPMorgan Sees $450 Billion AI Debt Blitz in 2027 Before Plateau
articles.summary: Companies will tap public high-grade debt markets for $450 billion next year to finance their artificial intelligence-related capital expenditures, even as a...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Companies will tap public high-grade debt markets for $450 billion next year to finance their artificial intelligence-related capital expenditures, even as a growth plateau looms for the burgeoning industry further down the road, according to analysts at JPMorgan Chase & Co.

The financing would be an increase from the $368 billion of global investment grade bond issuance for AI-focused companies this year, according to the bank.

Overall, AI-related capital spending will nearly double to $1.4 trillion in 2027 before leveling off in the following year, strategists led by Tarek Hamid and Nathaniel Rosenbaum wrote.

The strategists expect spending growth to slow sharply in 2028 as the industry settles into a steady run rate — a trend potentially foreshadowed by cautious commentary from Asian tech giants including Tencent and Alibaba.

"Due to the deceleration in overall industry growth rates, there will be a quarter in late 2027 or early 2028 when the outlook for next quarter's capital spending will be basically flat," the strategists wrote. "Whether the market reacts positively or negatively to that is anyone's guess."

The shift is set to create a more predictable debt supply for credit markets even as flat spending growth risks unsettling investor sentiment, the strategists said.

The bank expects the AI industry to build 151 gigawatts of data center capacity at a cost of $7 trillion between 2027 and 2031. Since most data center projects take multiple years to build and raise capital upfront, much of 2027's buildout is already paid for, meaning "funding in 2027 is really for 2028," they wrote.

In addition to the investment-grade debt, the bank expects companies to raise $65 billion through leveraged finance and $25 billion to $35 billion in securitized products in 2027.

With debt markets approaching their capacity limits at that scale, cash-rich hyperscalers are seen carrying more of the equity load, requiring $2.9 trillion of equity invested in the sector over the next five years, largely from organic cash flow.

At the same time, the type of asset being financed is shifting from physical data centers toward compute hardware.

"The mix of AI accelerator financing is likely to increase dramatically across public and private markets. By 2031, GPU financing needs could exceed power shell financing needs by a factor of four," the strategists wrote.

articles.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and 'key man' risks | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The credit rating agency may lower Nvidia's credit rating to AA-, the fourth-highest rating.
articles.body:
S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.

Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement .

The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.

Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.

In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported .

A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

articles.title: SoftBank Credit Risk Tops 500 Basis Points as AI Worries Mount
articles.summary: SoftBank Group Corp.’s credit risk surged above 500 basis points for the first time in about four years, raising the prospect of even higher funding costs as...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- SoftBank Group Corp.'s credit risk surged above 500 basis points for the first time in about four years, raising the prospect of even higher funding costs as the company presses ahead with massive investments in artificial intelligence.

SoftBank's five-year credit-default swap rose to 516 basis points as of 6:30 a.m. in Tokyo, the highest since October 2022, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The spread on a dollar bond it sold in September with a 9.75% coupon, the highest ever for one of its dollar notes, has widened about 40% since issuance to about 644 basis points.

The deterioration comes as the AI stock trade reverses, raising questions about the future valuation of OpenAI, in which SoftBank has invested $64.6 billion, and its ability to recoup that investment. Wider bond spreads could also make future issuance and refinancing more expensive.

"The broadening of the AI business isn't going to change, but monetization will take longer," said Masahito Sugawara, a senior strategist at Daiwa Securities Co. For AI firms relying on future cash flows to repay debt, delays in monetization could complicate refinancing and "lead investors to demand wider spreads," he said.

SoftBank's financial burden is already growing. Finance costs in the July-September quarter rose 2.6 times from a year earlier to ¥461.9 billion ($2.9 billion). It raised about ¥9 trillion during the quarter.

S&P Global Ratings said this month that key metrics were approaching the tolerance limits for its rating on SoftBank. It estimated the loan-to-value ratio has risen above 30%, approaching its 35% threshold for considering a downgrade.

Anthropic PBC shares fell below their initial public offering price less than four sessions after their record-setting debut. OpenAI has ruled out an IPO this year, adding uncertainty over the eventual valuation and monetization of SoftBank's massive investment.

articles.title: A BITS Pilani alumnus from UP quit his high-paying Microsoft job to build a Bengaluru-based AI startup, missing Rs 15 lakh voluntary exit offer by just a month; his venture joins OpenAI's partner network
articles.summary: A month can make all the difference between walking away with a Rs 15 lakh payout and leaving with nothing.
articles.body: A month can make all the difference between walking away with a Rs 15 lakh payout and leaving with nothing. But for a former Microsoft employee, missing out on the money has not changed his mind about quitting the tech giant. Atishay Jain, a BITS Pilani alumnus from Baraut in Uttar Pradesh, quit his high-paying job at Microsoft last month to pursue his entrepreneurial ambitions and build his own AI company. However, just a month after his exit, Microsoft reportedly introduced a voluntary exit offer that could have fetched him approximately Rs 15 lakh had he stayed on a little longer.In a LinkedIn post, Jain reflected on the timing of his resignation, writing, "I just missed out on ~Rs 15 lakh by quitting one month too early." He acknowledged that the amount was not insignificant, especially considering that he had already made up his mind to leave the company. "Rs 15 LAKH. For leaving a job I'd already decided to leave," he wrote.While the missed payout could have been a reason to second-guess his decision, Jain said he had no intention of looking back. "Does it sting? Oh yes. Do I regret leaving? Not for a second," he wrote. Jain, who describes himself as a former Microsoft and Nutanix employee, said his first month working full-time on his venture, ScaleWorks AI, had already brought three developments worth celebrating.The Bengaluru-based company, which positions itself as an AI transformation partner helping businesses work smarter and scale faster, became an official member of the OpenAI Partner Network. Jain also said he was accepted into Toptal, a global network of freelance professionals that describes its talent pool as representing the top 3% of applicants. articles.title: 'Some things you just don't take off the menu': Denny's stands by Jensen Huang after his Nvidia comeback
articles.summary: The San Jose diner's tribute to Nvidia's birthplace came down the night Huang resigned. Denny's put it back up days later, well before Nvidia's board brought...
articles.body:
When Jensen Huang lost his job as Nvidia's ( NVDA ) CEO earlier this month, he also lost his commemorative plaque at Denny's. Eleven days later, Huang returned to the helm of the chip giant to a rock-star welcome from cheering employees. His plaque, it turns out, beat him to the comeback.

Now the restaurant chain has a message for its most famous former dishwasher. "Some things you just don't take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them," Denny's wrote in a statement on social media on Wednesday.

Long before Huang became one of the most powerful people in the artificial intelligence industry, he was washing dishes at Denny's. Years later, he and two friends met at one of the chain's restaurants in San Jose, Calif., to discuss an idea that would become Nvidia, now ranked No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and the list's most valuable company when the ranking was published in June.

On Sept. 26, 2023, Denny's unveiled a plaque commemorating that very spot, calling it "The booth that launched a $1 trillion company."

The plaque came down on the evening of Nov. 12, an employee at the San Jose restaurant told SFGATE . That was the same day Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including an alleged affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials suspected of spying for China. Another restaurant worker told the New York Post that the decision to remove the plaque had come from the diner's "bosses."

Denny's reversed course well before Nvidia did. The chain says it learned of the removal on Friday, Nov. 13, and "put the plaque right back up where it belongs." By Nov. 14, a Denny's spokesperson had told SFGATE the plaque was being reinstalled. Denny's has not publicly explained why it was taken down in the first place.

Nvidia followed on Monday, Nov. 23, when its board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as president, CEO, and board member. The board said that, based on input from senior levels of the U.S. government, it was confident his return posed no national security risk. The reversal came after a public push from President Donald Trump , who has claimed credit for the decision.

On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that U.S. officials told congressional staff in a classified briefing that they had found no evidence China orchestrated the affair.

Huang was 15 when he got his first job at a Denny's in Portland, Ore. He spent five years as a dishwasher, busboy, and waiter, an experience he credits with helping him overcome his shyness and teaching him the value of hard work.

articles.title: Nvidia Reportedly Halts AI Chip Shipments To Southeast Asia As U.S. Tightens China Curbs
articles.summary: The reported halt in shipments comes just days after Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO following a scandal over his alleged extramarital affair wit...
articles.body:
Nvidia has instructed its manufacturing partners to halt shipments of servers equipped with its artificial intelligence chips to four Southeast Asian countries, the Financial Times reported Thursday, as the Trump administration moves to restrict Chinese AI companies' access to advanced American semiconductors amid heightened scrutiny of the chipmaker's business dealings in the region, following the controversy surrounding CEO Jensen Huang.

Citing three unnamed sources, the FT reported that Nvidia's manufacturing partners, including Dell and Supermicro, have informed customers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia that the chipmaking giant will not allow their servers to be shipped.

The report notes that it is unclear if the suspension is temporary to allow Nvidia and the server makers to address compliance with new U.S. export control rules.

The reported shipment freeze comes a week after new U.S. export restrictions went into effect, requiring companies to obtain licenses to ship advanced AI chips to the four Southeast Asian countries and Brazil, with exemptions for qualifying U.S.-based companies.

The move also follows the Nvidia board's decision to reinstate billionaire Jensen Huang as its CEO and the establishment of an independent National Security and Export Control Committee.

Bloomberg separately reported on Wednesday that the new restrictions have prompted lenders to pause billions in financing for Asian data center projects linked to Chinese technology giants, including ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent.

Are The New Chip Restrictions Affecting Chinese AI Firms?

Reuters reported on Thursday that China's Z.AI could delay the launch of its next flagship model, GLM-5.5. The company originally planned to release GLM-5.5 this month and later shifted its target to year-end, but the launch could now slip into the first quarter of 2027. The report also noted that rival Moonshot AI believes its six-month development cycle for models could double to a year or longer if it loses access to Nvidia chips hosted by overseas cloud providers. Its current flagship Kimi K3 model launched in July this year and the restrictions could push back the launch of its successor K4 to mid-2027. The chip restrictions come as the companies also face increased efforts by OpenAI and Anthropic to prevent distillation of their cutting-edge models. Distillation is a process that lets companies train models using outputs from more advanced models at a fraction of the cost.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn't a virtue | TechCrunch
articles.summary: On the same day that Anthropic entered the public market, a painstakingly human video game became one of most successful entertainment launches of all time.
articles.body:
It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week.

GTA VI launched as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ( $2.9 billion ) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ( $2 billion ).

The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI.

Even the biggest workaholics among us – startup founders – scheduled time off to play the game, including Spiry co-founder Dima Beseda , who told TechCrunch, “I reshuffled my workload to free up time around the weekends and even booked vitamin IV drips to keep my energy up.”

Yet some players felt a sense of anticipatory nostalgia as they wiped away a layer of dust on their Xbox to play the game they’d been looking forward to since they were kids.

“We do have a view that GTA is likely to be the last game of its kind to be made this way,” Ben Feder , managing partner at TIRTA Ventures and former CEO of Rockstar parent company Take-Two Interactive, told TechCrunch.

That’s because GTA VI was created entirely without generative AI .

“We’re kind of at this technological moment where this way of developing has sort of reached its natural frontier,” Feder said. “I don’t think you can say that games like this will always be around.”

As millions of people immersed themselves in Vice City, the tech industry witnessed another long-awaited moment: Anthropic became the first major AI lab to go public. At Nasdaq HQ, Anthropic executives gathered to celebrate the Claude maker’s $81.3 billion IPO. At virtually the same moment that Anthropic broke the record for the largest IPO ever, GTA VI was also breaking records with the highest-rated and best-selling game launch of all time.

But when the Anthropic team rang the bell on Thursday, the sound also signaled the end of an era in video game development, and perhaps even in the arts at large.

The AI industry operates with efficiency as its north star. The promise of this technology is that we will be able to automate so much work that we can expand the capabilities of humanity, avoiding needless time spent tinkering with ultimately fruitless ideas. Instead, a prompt goes into an LLM, and a response is spat out.

This technological revolution exploded into the world with some soul-crushing side effects: children are inundated with mind-numbing slop on YouTube, lawyers cite nonexistent cases in court, and tech companies like Meta lay off tens of thousands of people as part of a corporate-branded “ Year of Efficiency. ” But against the backdrop of the AI industry’s first major IPO, Rockstar has unveiled a game that about 5,000 people labored over for more than a decade.

The final product is breathtaking, looking so lifelike that it can be hard to distinguish gameplay footage from real life. These sprawling open-world games are usually made possible by procedurally generating new landscapes and objects, but Rockstar has taken the time to painstakingly craft every detail of the world, even developing 30,000 different nonplayable characters with unique appearances and personalities.

The video game industry is already grappling with the threat of AI. Google’s Project Genie , which launched earlier this year, allows users to create and wander around 3D worlds generated from prompts to an LLM. The stock prices of several video game companies faltered around the time of Project Genie’s release, perhaps because of investors’ uncertainty about the future relevance of video game developers.

“The notion that somehow new tools would allow an individual to push a button and generate a hit, market a hit, and bring it to many millions of consumers around the world, it’s a laughable notion,” Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said at the time. “It’s just never been the case with entertainment.”

Zelnick’s fellow tech CEOs see different future, though. On a Meta earnings call this year, CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised that, “soon, you’ll have an AI that understands you and [can] even generate great personalized content for you.”

Elon Musk even went as far as proposing that a game like GTA VI could be made with AI.

“You won’t even have to ask,” Musk wrote on X . “AI will figure what video game you’d like best.”

This is the paradox of “ Grandthropic ” week. GTA VI is so impressively vast and captivating because its developers could make mistakes, experiment, and rework ideas, even if that meant delaying the game (twice). GTA VI was incubated with the exact inefficiencies that investors hope AI companies like Anthropic can help eradicate.

“Plenty of fantastic art — video games and elsewhere — almost by definition has to be created slowly, and there’s something to having that kind of inefficiency around it,” Feder said. “Creative output requires deletion, right? Getting to kind of a masterpiece oftentimes requires an enormous amount of deletion. And when you’re talking about a game of the kind of complexity we’re talking about, that kind of deletion ends up being very expensive, and it is by definition not efficient.”

GTA VI reeks of its own humanity – every small detail is loaded with intention, but it’s this impressive precision that keeps the world abuzz, triggering the kind of monocultural moment that has become increasingly rare in a media landscape that revolves around highly personalized social media algorithms.

The game forces the player to slow down, which is either frustrating or genius, depending on your sense of humor. People waited more than three presidential terms for the next installment in a high-octane action franchise, only to download a 212 GB behemoth of a game in which your earliest missions involve driving around doing errands and putting up drywall to make your girlfriend happy. Don’t worry — there are still car chases and shootouts — but in a moment when AI feels suffocating, GTA VI is such an artistic achievement that it is reaching audiences that don’t even like violent video games.

The ultimate fantasy of GTA VI is no longer to role-play as a criminal — the fantasy is just taking your time to relish the mundane and explore an expansive world that developers were given the time and space to perfect.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says AI is changing what it means to be smart, explains why empathy, life experience and the ability to ‘Feel the Vibe’ matter
articles.summary: For years, being considered intelligent often meant being good at mathematics, solving difficult problems, understanding technology or writing computer
articles.body: For years, being considered intelligent often meant being good at mathematics, solving difficult problems, understanding technology or writing computer code. But as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly capable of performing such tasks, could the qualities we associate with intelligence be changing? Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang believes they are.During a conversation with Jodi Shelton on the 'A Bit Personal' podcast, Huang was asked a seemingly straightforward question: Who is the smartest person he has ever met? Rather than naming an individual, he used the opportunity to explain why he believes people have a limited understanding of intelligence."I can't answer that question," he responded, before challenging the conventional idea that intelligence is primarily about technical knowledge and problem-solving. His answer offered an interesting perspective on how human abilities could become even more valuable as AI advances.Why traditional measures of intelligence may no longer be enoughHuang explained that people have traditionally associated intelligence with the ability to understand complex subjects, solve problems and demonstrate strong technical skills. However, he believes these abilities are becoming less distinctive as AI systems improve. "The definition of smart is somebody who's intelligent, solve problems, technical. But I find that that's a commodity," he explained.He pointed to software programming as an example. For a long time, coding was considered one of the most intellectually demanding professions. Yet AI tools are increasingly capable of writing code, identifying errors and assisting with complicated programming tasks.Huang questioned this traditional understanding of intelligence, suggesting that technical problem-solving alone may not be enough to distinguish people in the future. His argument was not that technical knowledge has become unimportant. Rather, he believes the qualities that make someone truly valuable are expanding beyond what machines can increasingly perform.The combination of technical knowledge and human empathyInstead of focusing entirely on academic achievements or technical expertise, Huang offered his own definition of intelligence. He believes truly smart people possess a combination of technical understanding and human empathy. He explained that such individuals can understand what others are thinking without everything being explicitly communicated. They can recognise situations that others might overlook and anticipate challenges before they become obvious.In his words, intelligence involves "the ability to infer the unspoken, the around-the-corner, the unknowables." This ability to understand people and situations beyond the information immediately available is something Huang considers particularly valuable.For instance, someone managing a team might notice that an employee is struggling even when they have not directly expressed it. Similarly, a business leader might recognise early signs of a problem before it becomes visible in reports or performance figures. Such decisions require more than analysing numbers. They involve experience, observation, judgement and an understanding of human behaviour. For Huang, these qualities represent an important part of what intelligence should mean in an increasingly technology-driven world.What does it mean to ‘feel the vibe’?One of the most interesting parts of Huang's explanation was his reference to something he described as 'feeling the vibe'. He suggested that people who can sense potential problems before they arise often rely on a combination of different abilities. He explained that this instinct comes from "data analysis, first principles, life experience, wisdom" and the ability to sense other people.In other words, it is not simply about making decisions based on feelings. It involves combining available information with experience, logical thinking and an understanding of people. Someone with this ability may recognise that something is not right even when there is no obvious evidence yet. Their experience helps them connect different signals and identify possibilities that others may miss.Huang believes people who can anticipate challenges in this way will become increasingly valuable. He also made an interesting observation about conventional academic assessments. According to him, someone with these qualities might actually perform poorly on a standardised examination such as the SAT.His point was that examination scores cannot necessarily capture every form of intelligence, particularly qualities such as empathy, judgement and the ability to understand situations that have no straightforward answers. The conversation offers a thought-provoking perspective on how people might need to rethink intelligence as AI becomes more capable.For students, professionals and those entering the workforce, the message is worth considering. Learning technical skills remains important, but developing the ability to understand people, think independently and make sound decisions could be just as valuable. Huang's answer also leaves readers with an interesting question: In a world where machines can increasingly solve complex problems, will the ability to understand what cannot easily be measured become one of the most important forms of intelligence?You use AI every day. articles.title: Anthropic Shares Jump After Volatile First Week Since IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic PBC shares climbed above their $83 initial public offering price as the artificial intelligence lab looked to end its first calendar week on the Na...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC shares climbed above their $83 initial public offering price as the artificial intelligence lab looked to end its first calendar week on the Nasdaq after its record-setting debut on a positive note.

The stock increased about 11% from the previous session to $91.90 each as of 12:05 p.m. on Friday in New York, the highest intraday level since Monday, putting it on track to end a two-day streak of closing below the IPO price. Anthropic joined a broader rally in a shortened trading day following the Thanksgiving holiday, as risk appetite returned after a slump.

Concern over the pace of AI spending had roiled tech stocks in the lead-up to the Claude Code maker's record $119.5 billion first-time share sale, and spread to Anthropic's shares after Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang's return to the chipmaker as investors weighed the potential impact of the controversy on the AI ecosystem.

The trading gives the Dario Amodei-led company a market capitalization of roughly $1.7 trillion. That's below the peak of more than $2 trillion during the firm's debut on Nov. 19, when shares touched $115.10 before retreating.

The uneven debut has drawn scrutiny around the IPO's execution. Some investors have questioned the decision to allow Anthropic's underwriting banks to exercise the so-called over-allotment option after the first day, rather than preserving the ability to support the stock.

Others drew attention to the slug of as many as 315 million shares released from a lockup agreement on insiders on the first trading day, as part of the company's year-long staggered lockup releases, according to its prospectus.

A further tranche of as many as 303 million shares held by insiders are expected to become available for sale on Dec. 15, the prospectus shows. Also in December, indexes including the Nasdaq 100 could add Anthropic shares, leading to a wave of buying from tracking funds.

The rapid adoption of products such as Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent for software developers, and the company's revenue run rate of $81 billion at the end of October, made for a powerful sales pitch for the company's IPO. That helped investors overlook the company's committed spending nearing $901 billion through 2045.

articles.title: Trump’s AI Gambit Fuels Wild Thanksgiving Week on Wall Street
articles.summary: The message from Washington this week was unmistakable: America must do whatever it takes to win the artificial-intelligence race with China, and the governm...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The message from Washington this week was unmistakable: America must do whatever it takes to win the artificial-intelligence race with China, and the government is prepared to intervene to make it happen.

A jittery Wall Street has cheered the message. Yet the wild swings in financial markets show the limits of investor conviction.

President Donald Trump's intervention to bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia Corp. restored to the helm not just one of the biggest AI evangelists but one of the chief financiers of its expansion. Technology stocks soared, sank and rallied again, with a 1.6% jump in the S&P 500 Friday capping a week of gains across risk assets.

The recent turbulence, which Trump acknowledged Thursday had briefly left him concerned, was an unusually intense bout of the volatility that has gripped Wall Street for months as the financial and economic stakes of the AI boom have grown.

"There was a tacit admission – or maybe not even so tacit – that Nvidia's too big to fail, Jensen is too big to fail, and if you're well enough connected with the powers that be, you'll get bailed out to some extent," said Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers.

The euphoria over Huang's return had barely lasted a day before stocks started sliding again, while fresh tariff threats from the Trump administration added to market swings.

An average of 21 billion shares changed hands daily in the first three sessions, the busiest start to Thanksgiving week in Bloomberg data going back to 2008. The Nasdaq 100 Index had alternated between weekly gains and losses of more than 3% for four straight weeks, something not seen since July 2022.

Through Wednesday's close, a gauge of expected volatility in the Nasdaq 100 had averaged 33 in November, putting it on course for its highest monthly reading since April 2022 and the highest for any November since the global financial crisis. Relative to a diversified portfolio of global stocks, bonds and commodities, US equities have been this volatile only once before since the pandemic, going by 30-day measures of realized volatility.

At the heart of the whiplash is a question that even the full political weight of the US government cannot answer: Who will emerge as the winners and losers from one of the biggest investment booms in history? The prospect of higher borrowing costs only compounds the dilemma, raising the bar for those investments to pay off.

articles.title: OpenAI Says Apple Pressured Suppliers to Shun Its Devices
articles.summary: The trade-secrets fight between OpenAI and Apple Inc. is widening, with the artificial intelligence company accusing the iPhone maker of undermining its supp...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The trade-secrets fight between OpenAI and Apple Inc. is widening, with the artificial intelligence company accusing the iPhone maker of undermining its supplier relationships and using unfair employment agreements to prevent talent from jumping ship.

OpenAI filed counterclaims against Apple on Friday in federal court in San Jose, California, transforming the lawsuit Apple brought earlier against OpenAI into a two-way battle over the companies' intellectual property.

The case has overshadowed OpenAI's bid to sell its own devices, a move that would put it in competition with the iPhone maker. Former Apple design guru Jony Ive is helping the AI company develop a family of products, starting with what's expected to be a doughnut-shaped smart speaker.

"Apple has responded to OpenAI's anticipated entry into the hardware market by unlawfully pressuring vendors not to work with OpenAI and using expansive employment restraints to limit OpenAI's access to talented engineers," OpenAI said in the filing. "Apple's power over suppliers and engineers cannot lawfully be used to exclude competing purchasers and employers from the market."

Apple did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.

Apple in July sued OpenAI and Tang Tan, the AI company's chief hardware officer, alleging the ChatGPT maker orchestrated a campaign to steal trade secrets via job candidates and hires from Apple. The companies had earlier collaborated to integrate ChatGPT directly into iPhone, iPad and Mac software, only to see that relationship cool more recently.

In the new counterclaims, OpenAI alleges Apple unfairly pressures industry suppliers to "identify their OpenAI projects and the names, locations, and assignments of workers with Apple experience."

Apple then seeks to exclude workers with OpenAI experience from doing further work for the iPhone maker, effectively discouraging suppliers from committing workers to OpenAI projects, according to the filing.

Another industry supplier that provides specialist finishing services moved its manufacturing work for OpenAI products to the night shift to avoid overlapping with work for Apple, increasing costs for OpenAI, according to the filing. The supplier did so under pressure from Apple, OpenAI says.
